title: Organophosphate and carbamate poisoning
subject: toxicology
summary: Resuscitate, then give atropine in doubling doses every 5 minutes until the chest is clear, heart rate is above 80 and systolic BP above 80 mmHg; maintain with an infusion of 10 to 20% of the loading dose per hour, consider pralidoxime, avoid routine lavage, and watch for intermediate syndrome.

sections.title: Recognise
items: History of pesticide ingestion (often with a solvent or kerosene-like smell) with a cholinergic crisis: miosis, salivation, lacrimation, sweating, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, vomiting, diarrhoea, urination, bradycardia, hypotension.
Nicotinic features: fasciculations, weakness and paralysis. Tachycardia, hypertension and mydriasis can also occur and do not exclude OP poisoning.
CNS features: agitation, confusion, coma and central respiratory depression. Death is mainly from respiratory failure.
Low plasma (butyryl) cholinesterase confirms exposure but does not grade severity; red cell acetylcholinesterase reflects severity better. Never wait for levels to treat.
Carbamates cause the same syndrome, usually shorter lived; treat with atropine in the same way.

sections.title: Resuscitation and atropinisation
items: Left lateral, head-down position; suction secretions; high-flow oxygen; intubate if airway or breathing is compromised. Avoid suxamethonium (prolonged paralysis); use a non-depolarising relaxant.
Record heart rate, BP, pupil size, sweating and chest auscultation, then give atropine 1 to 3 mg IV bolus according to severity (for example 1.8 to 3 mg as 3 to 5 ampoules of 0.6 mg).

Reassess after 5 minutes. If the targets are not met, give double the previous dose, and keep doubling every 5 minutes (for example 2, 4, 8, 16 mg). Once parameters improve, stop doubling and give similar or smaller doses.

Atropinisation targets: clear chest (no bronchorrhoea or wheeze), heart rate above 80/min, systolic BP above 80 mmHg; sweating usually stops. Tachycardia is not a contraindication, and pupil size is not a target.
IV 0.9% saline to keep systolic BP above 80 mmHg and urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/h. Vasopressor if hypotension persists despite atropine and fluids.
Remove contaminated clothing and wash skin with soap and water; staff wear gloves.

sections.title: Maintenance atropine and oximes
items: Once stable, start an atropine infusion giving 10 to 20% of the total loading dose per hour. Review often: returning cholinergic signs need a bolus and a higher rate.
Atropine toxicity (agitation, confusion, hyperthermia, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention, very dilated pupils): stop the infusion for 30 to 60 minutes, then restart at a lower rate.

Pralidoxime (WHO regimen): 30 mg/kg IV over 20 to 30 minutes (about 2 g in adults), then 8 mg/kg/h (about 0.5 g/h). Never give as a rapid bolus. Continue until atropine has not been needed for 12 to 24 hours and the patient is extubated.

Oxime evidence is conflicting: a large Sri Lankan RCT of the WHO regimen showed no survival benefit, while an Indian RCT (2 g load then 1 g/h for 48 hours) reported less atropine use and ventilation. Give early if used, as reactivation fails once enzyme has aged.

Agitation: exclude atropine toxicity and hypoxia, then sedate with diazepam 5 to 10 mg IV, repeated as needed. Diazepam is also first line for seizures. Avoid physical restraint in a hot environment (hyperthermia).

sections.title: Decontamination
items: Oxygen, atropine and airway care come first. No form of gastric decontamination has been shown to improve outcome in OP poisoning.
Gastric lavage only after stabilisation, soon after a large ingestion, and only if intubated or conscious and cooperative. Never induce vomiting.
Single or multiple-dose activated charcoal showed no benefit in a large RCT in pesticide poisoning; it is not routinely recommended.

sections.title: Monitoring and intermediate syndrome
items: Review heart rate, BP, chest, pupils, sweating, bowel sounds, temperature and consciousness frequently to titrate atropine.
Intermediate syndrome: weakness of neck flexors, proximal limbs, cranial nerves and respiratory muscles, typically 24 to 96 hours after poisoning, often after the cholinergic crisis has settled.
Test neck flexion strength regularly (lift the head off the bed against pressure). Any weakness: measure tidal volume every 4 hours.
Intubate and ventilate if tidal volume is below 5 mL/kg, vital capacity below 15 mL/kg, there are apnoeic spells, or PaO2 is below 60 mmHg (8 kPa) on FiO2 above 60%.
Fat-soluble OPs (for example fenthion) can cause recurrent cholinergic crises for days; keep monitoring after stopping atropine and re-treat if needed.
Warn about delayed polyneuropathy (distal weakness 2 to 3 weeks later) with some OPs.

sections.title: Escalate to ICU
items: Need for intubation, high or rising atropine requirement, persistent hypotension, reduced consciousness, or any neck flexor weakness.
Suspected aspiration pneumonia, which is common after reduced consciousness or lavage.
From a peripheral centre, transfer only after initial atropinisation, with atropine, suction and airway equipment for the journey; never delay atropine while arranging oximes or transfer.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Slow fixed-dose atropine regimens that take hours to atropinise; use dose doubling every 5 minutes.
Stopping atropine because of tachycardia or dilated pupils when the chest is still wet.
Gastric lavage before resuscitation and atropine.
Relaxing monitoring after the cholinergic phase: intermediate syndrome can kill a conscious patient.
Using suxamethonium for intubation.

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.dose: 1 to 3 mg IV bolus, doubled every 5 minutes until atropinised; then infusion of 10 to 20% of the total loading dose per hour
drugs.notes: Titrate to a clear chest, heart rate above 80/min and systolic BP above 80 mmHg.

drugs.name: Pralidoxime chloride
drugs.dose: 30 mg/kg IV over 20 to 30 minutes (about 2 g), then 8 mg/kg/h (about 0.5 g/h)
drugs.notes: Continue until atropine not needed for 12 to 24 hours and extubated. Benefit uncertain; never a rapid bolus.

drugs.name: Diazepam
drugs.dose: 5 to 10 mg IV, repeat as needed
drugs.notes: Agitation after excluding atropine toxicity; seizures.

drugs.name: 0.9% saline
drugs.dose: IV boluses to keep systolic BP above 80 mmHg and urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/h
